text:
A: Hi! Hello, can you hear me okay?
B: Hello! Yes, perfectly. Karim. You must be Hannah.
A: Yeah, hi! How are you doing?
B: I'm good, thanks. I'm on my fourth one now, I feel like a speed dating professional. How are you?
A: I'm good, thanks, bit knackered. I've been on school placement all week. I'm doing a PGCE, primary, in Exeter.
B: Okay, I have to ask, because I'm doing a sort of survey in my head. Do you have a dog?
A: [laughs] Yeah, a cocker spaniel. Why?
B: What's it called?
A: Biscuit.
B: No. No way. That's the third Biscuit today. I'm not even joking. Two cockapoos and now you.
A: Stop it! Sorry, that's so funny. Is it a really common name? I didn't name him, my brother did when he was about fifteen.
B: Apparently it's the only name in England. We don't have a dog. My daughter wants one. If we get one, I'm calling it something else purely out of principle.
A: [laughs] How old's your daughter?
B: Lina's eleven, and my son Yusuf is fifteen. Lina's teaching me TikTok at the moment, which mostly involves her laughing at me.
A: Aw, that's sweet, though. Eleven's such a nice age. I'm in Year 1 now, so they're five, six. One of them told someone my ponytail looked like a horse's bottom this week.
B: [laughs] That's honest feedback. You can't get that in an office. My staff are too scared to tell me anything that direct.
A: What do you do?
B: Commercial director at a food import company in Birmingham. Middle Eastern, Mediterranean, Turkish snacks, all that. I bring jars home and make the family test them. My mum tells me most of them are rubbish compared to what she makes.
A: Oh, that's a fun job, though. I'll be honest, I'm a bit boring with food. I'm very much the korma end of the menu. Is it all spicy stuff?
B: No, no, a lot of people think that. Most Iraqi food isn't hot at all. It's more like, warm spices. Cinnamon, cardamom, lots of rice. My mum's dolma, you'd love it, it's basically stuffed vine leaves with rice and lemon. Not scary.
A: Okay, I'd try that. I'd try the not-scary version.
B: That's all I ask. Is it your mum who cooks at home, or you?
A: My mum mostly, I'm back living with my parents. Her Sunday roast is the best thing in the world. I do bolognese or fajitas when it's my turn.
B: Sunday's my mum's day as well, she comes round to ours. She speaks Arabic to the kids and they answer her in English. Every week. It drives her mad.
A: Aw. Do they understand her, though?
B: Mostly. I worry a bit that it'll fade, to be honest. You don't think about it until it's going.
A: That's sort of what teaching is, though, isn't it? Little and often. Like, just keep talking to them in it, even if they answer in English.
